title: Inside Neo4j: native graph storage, memory and clustering
goal: By the end you can take one real database apart with this track's ideas: explain how Neo4j lays a graph out as fixed-size, linked records and why a hop never needs an index, size its page cache (a buffer pool) and heap, describe what its transaction log (a write-ahead log) and checkpoints do in a crash, back up a Community server, and say what a cluster adds.

warmup.q: Neo4j has just loaded 37 relationships and confirmed every commit. How big is the relationship store file on disk at that moment?
options: 8,192 bytes: one page
0 bytes
It depends on the relationship index
warmup.why: It's 0 bytes, as the third section shows. A commit is durable once it is in the transaction log; the store files are written later, at a checkpoint (every 15 minutes or 100,000 transactions, or at shutdown). One page, 8,192 bytes, is what it became after the server stopped cleanly, which makes it the tempting answer. And relationships have no index to find them.

sections.h: A hop is a multiplication, not a search
sections.body:
This lesson is a case study: one real database, taken apart with the ideas of this track. Neo4j stores a graph as records in pages, like the heap files of lesson 2, except that every record has the same size. It reads them through its own page cache, a buffer pool like lesson 3's. It makes commits durable with a transaction log, the write-ahead log of lesson 6, and replays it after a crash. Its indexes are lesson 4's B+trees. What's new is how the records point at each other.

Node 2 of the fraud graph from the Data models track's lesson on Neo4j and Cypher lives at byte 30 of a file called `neostore.nodestore.db`. Relationship 28 lives at byte 952 of `neostore.relationshipstore.db`. Neo4j finds both without an index: 2 x 15 = 30, and 28 x 34 = 952. That multiplication is what that lesson called index-free adjacency. This lesson opens the files and looks.

Start with the obvious way to store a graph: a table of nodes and a link table of relationships, with a B+tree index on each end of the link (lesson 4). To find an account's relationships, the database descends the index on `from` and the index on `to`. At 100,000 rows each tree is 3 levels deep, at 10 million it's 4, and every level compares keys on a page. The cost of one hop grows, slowly, with the size of the whole graph.

Now make every record the same size and give it a number. Record N then starts at byte N x size, and finding it is arithmetic. Neo4j's record format does exactly that. A node record is 15 bytes: an in-use flag, the id of the node's first relationship, the id of its first property record, its labels, and a flag. A relationship record is 34 bytes: the two node ids, the type, and four pointers. Property records are 41 bytes, with room for four 8-byte blocks, so small values fit inline. Neo4j moves files in 8 KB pages, and the `aligned` format pads the end of each page so a record never straddles two: a page holds 546 node records or 240 relationship records.

The four pointers are what make it a graph. Each node's relationships form a doubly linked list, threaded through the relationship records themselves. A relationship belongs to two lists, one per end, so it carries a previous and a next pointer for each. New relationships go in at the head, so a chain reads newest first. The head has no previous record, and Neo4j stores the chain's length in that field instead: a node's degree costs two reads.

**A Neo4j server is fixed-size records in files, a page cache that keeps those files in memory, and a transaction log in front of both: a query finds its start through an index, then hops from record to record by multiplying ids.** The rest of this lesson adds the page cache, the log and the cluster to that picture.

Two refinements matter at scale. A node with thousands of relationships would make "outgoing transfers only" read all of them, so once a node passes `db.relationship_grouping_threshold` (50) Neo4j splits its chain into relationship groups, one chain per type and direction. And there's a second layout. Since 5.22, new Enterprise databases default to the `block` format, which keeps a node's labels, properties and relationships together in one 128-byte block, so most nodes can be read from one place instead of three files, and keeps the relationships of very dense nodes in a B+tree. Community Edition, which this lab runs, stays on `aligned`: `neo4j-admin database info` reports `record-aligned-1.1`.

sections.h: The page cache holds the store, the heap runs the queries
sections.body:
A hop is one multiplication and one read, and the read decides the speed. From memory it takes about 100 nanoseconds. From an SSD it takes about 100 microseconds, a thousand times longer. A fraud walk that reads 2,000 records takes 0.2 ms when every page is in memory and can take 200 ms when every read goes to the disk. So Neo4j keeps the store files in memory, in its own page cache.

The page cache is a buffer pool, the same idea as lesson 3. At startup Neo4j allocates `server.memory.pagecache.size` bytes outside the Java heap and divides it into 8 KB pages. A record read asks the cache for the page that holds it. On a hit, the read is a memory access. On a miss, Neo4j reads the page from the file, evicting a cold page if the cache is full. Changed pages stay dirty in the cache until a checkpoint writes them back (the next section). Neo4j manages this memory itself instead of leaving it to the kernel's page cache from the Operating systems track, so it decides what stays in memory and when dirty pages reach the disk. Its range indexes live in the same cache, because they are B+trees in pages too.

The Java heap holds everything else: query plans and the plan cache, the rows a query is working on, and every change a transaction makes until it commits. A `CREATE` of 2,000 relationships keeps all 2,000 in the heap until it commits. The garbage collector pauses grow with the heap, and above about 31 GB the JVM loses compressed object pointers, so a bigger heap holds less per gigabyte.

So size them for different things. The page cache should hold the whole store plus its indexes, with room to grow: Neo4j's manual takes the store size and adds 20%, so 35 GB becomes 42 GB. The heap should be big enough for the queries and transactions that run at the same time, typically a few GB to 31 GB, with the initial size equal to the maximum (`server.memory.heap.initial_size` and `server.memory.heap.max_size`) so the JVM never resizes it. Leave the operating system at least a gigabyte, more if you use full-text or vector indexes, which are Lucene files cached by the kernel.

`neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation` prints a starting split for a machine dedicated to Neo4j, and `--memory` asks about a machine you don't have yet. Treat it as a starting point. It doesn't know how big your store will be, so check the page cache against the store yourself.

sections.h: Every commit goes to the transaction log first
sections.body:
Right after the fraud graph is loaded, `neostore.relationshipstore.db` is 0 bytes long. All 37 relationships are in the page cache and in a 15,715-byte file called `neostore.transaction.db.0`. Neo4j wrote the log first and the store not at all.

Here's why. One commit can change pages in four or five files: the node store, the relationship store, the property store, an index. Writing them all at commit would mean scattered writes on every transaction, and a crash halfway through would leave half a relationship on disk. So Neo4j does what lesson 6 describes. At commit it appends the transaction's changes to the transaction log, one sequential write, and forces it to disk with fsync (the Operating systems track's lesson on the page cache and fsync). Then it applies the same changes to the pages in the page cache. The commit is durable once the log is on disk, even though the store files are behind.

The store catches up at a checkpoint. Neo4j writes every dirty page back to its file and records in `checkpoint.0` how far the store files are now complete. By default it checks every 15 minutes or every 100,000 transactions (`db.checkpoint.interval.time` and `db.checkpoint.interval.tx`), and it always checkpoints on a clean shutdown. After a crash, the store files are as old as the last checkpoint, so at startup Neo4j replays the log from there: recovery. The Try-it crashes the server on purpose and watches it replay.

The log is also how other things catch up: Enterprise's differential backups and cluster members read it. Neo4j rotates a log file at 256 MiB (`db.tx_log.rotation.size`) and keeps 2 days and 2 GB of them by default (`db.tx_log.rotation.retention_policy`). Put `data/transactions` on a fast disk, because every commit waits for it.

The `schema/index` folder holds the indexes, and they answer the one question a walk can't: where to start. Every database is created with two token lookup indexes, from a label to its nodes and from a type to its relationships. That's what `NodeByLabelScan` reads in the plans of the Data models track's Neo4j lesson. A uniqueness constraint on `Account.id` adds a range index, a B+tree in its own file under `schema/index/range-1.0`, and turns the start into `NodeUniqueIndexSeek`. Once the walk has its first node, it never touches an index again.

sections.h: One server: neo4j.conf, the data folder and neo4j-admin
sections.body:
Everything so far ran on one server, and setting one up comes down to one file, one folder and one tool.

The file is `conf/neo4j.conf`. It holds plain `key=value` settings, and the ones you set on day one are few:

```properties
# listen on every interface (the default is localhost only)
server.default_listen_address=0.0.0.0
# the address clients and routing tables are given
server.default_advertised_address=graph-1.internal
# Bolt, for drivers and cypher-shell; HTTP, for the API and the browser
server.bolt.listen_address=:7687
server.http.listen_address=:7474
server.memory.heap.initial_size=8g
server.memory.heap.max_size=8g
server.memory.pagecache.size=24g
server.directories.transaction.logs.root=/fastdisk/transactions
db.tx_log.rotation.retention_policy=2 days 2G
dbms.security.auth_enabled=true
```

In Docker you don't edit the file. Every `NEO4J_` environment variable becomes a setting, with `_` in place of each dot and `__` in place of each `_`, so `NEO4J_server_memory_pagecache_size` is `server.memory.pagecache.size`. That's how the lab's `env/neo4j.yml` sets its memory, and the Try-it shows the lines it produced.

The folder is `data/`. `data/databases/<name>/` holds one database's store files and its `schema/index/` folder, `data/transactions/<name>/` its transaction log, and `data/dumps/` the archives `neo4j-admin` writes. Next to it, `logs/` has `neo4j.log`, `debug.log` (where the recovery line was), `query.log` and `security.log`. A Neo4j server always has two databases: `system`, which holds users, roles and the list of databases, and the default user database, `neo4j`.

The tool is `neo4j-admin`, and its jobs follow from the files. `neo4j-admin database import full` builds store files directly from CSV files while the database is offline, without going through transactions, which makes it the fastest way to do the first load of hundreds of millions of records. `dump` writes one database to a single compressed archive and `load` puts one back; both need the database offline. `info` reads a store's format and whether it needs recovery, `check` verifies the store is consistent, and `migrate` moves a database to another store format.

Community Edition, the free one this lab runs, stops there, and its limits are plain. It runs one standalone server with one user database: `CREATE DATABASE` fails. It has no online backup, so you back it up by stopping the server and running `dump`. It has no clustering and no `block` format. Enterprise Edition adds online `neo4j-admin database backup` and `restore`, full and differential, and the cluster in the next section.

sections.h: Clustering: primaries agree with Raft, secondaries scale reads
sections.body:
A single server is a single failure. If it crashes, the fraud graph is down until it restarts and replays its log. If its disk dies, you're back to the last dump. Neo4j's answer is a cluster, and it's Enterprise only.

A cluster is a set of servers, and each database has copies on some of them. A copy in primary mode takes part in writes. The primaries of a database form a Raft group. Raft is a consensus protocol that the Consistency and consensus track builds step by step; here you need only its central rule, that a write counts as committed once a majority of the group has it in its log. The primaries elect one as the writer, Raft's leader, and every write transaction goes to it. The writer appends the transaction to its log, sends it to the other primaries, and commits once a majority have it in their logs: 2 of 3. The others apply it from there.

The arithmetic is Raft's. To survive F failed primaries you need 2F + 1: three tolerate one failure, five tolerate two. The manual caps a database at 11 primaries, and says not to go near that, because every write waits for more servers. If a majority is lost, the database stops taking writes, which is the price of never losing a committed one.

A copy in secondary mode never votes. It pulls the transaction log from the primaries, asynchronously, applies it, and serves reads. Secondaries scale out reads, up to 20 per database, and losing one costs throughput and nothing else. Because they pull, they can be a little behind.

The driver hides the topology. With a `neo4j://` address, the driver connects to any server, fetches a routing table that lists which servers can write, read and route, and caches it for its TTL (300 seconds). Then it sends each write transaction to the writer and spreads read transactions over the readers. A `bolt://` address means one specific server, no routing: point it at a follower and writes fail. To read your own write from a secondary, the driver passes a bookmark naming the transaction you just committed, and the cluster runs the read only on a server that has applied it: read-your-writes, which the Replication track's lesson on replication lag treats properly.

Setting one up adds two settings per server to the `neo4j.conf` of the last section: the list of every server's discovery endpoint (port 6000) and how many primaries new databases get. The advertised address starts to matter too, because it's what the routing table hands to drivers. The compare block shows the difference.

For the fraud graph the choice is about downtime. A Community server fed from Kafka can be rebuilt by replaying the topic, which costs hours, not data. If the authorization path reads risk flags from the graph, run three primaries.

refs.title: Neo4j Java Driver Manual: connection URIs and routing

analogy: Neo4j's store is a warehouse with numbered shelves of identical bins. Bin 952 is always at the same spot, so a picker walks straight to it without a catalogue. Each bin holds one relationship and a note saying which bin holds the next relationship for each of its two owners, so a picker follows notes from bin to bin. The page cache is the stock kept at the packing desk: a bin fetched from the desk takes a second, one fetched from the far end of the warehouse takes a minute. The transaction log is the clipboard where every change is written before anyone moves stock, so after a power cut the night shift can redo the day from the clipboard. The analogy breaks on the catalogue: a real warehouse would still need one to find a product by name, and Neo4j does too, but only for the first bin of each walk.
in_your_world: If your fraud team runs Neo4j, size it like you size Oracle's SGA, from the data. Count accounts, devices and transfers, multiply by 15, 34 and 41 bytes, add indexes and 20%, and give that to `server.memory.pagecache.size`. Keep the heap at 31 GB or less, the way you would for any JVM service. The transaction log is Neo4j's redo log: put `data/transactions` on fast storage, because every `MERGE` your Kafka consumer commits waits for its fsync. If the graph is a copy rebuilt from Kafka topics, Community and a nightly `dump` may be enough. If the authorization path reads risk flags from it inside a 120 ms budget, buy Enterprise, run three primaries, and connect with `neo4j://` so the driver follows the writer through failovers.
mistake: The most common mistake is leaving Neo4j's memory at its defaults, or setting a huge heap and a small page cache because "Java needs memory". It works in testing, where the store is a few hundred MB and fits anywhere. In production the store is 80 GB, the page cache holds a fraction of it, and every walk that leaves the hot part of the graph reads 8 KB pages from disk one at a time, so a 5 ms ring query takes seconds. A 64 GB heap makes it worse: longer GC pauses and no compressed oops. The fix is to measure the store (`neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation` prints its size, as does `du` on `data/databases`), set the page cache to that plus 20%, keep the heap at or below 31 GB with initial equal to max, and leave the operating system its share.

worked.title: Size the fraud graph's server from its record counts

steps.say: Start from the counts the fraud team expects in a year: 120 million nodes (50 million accounts, 70 million devices and phones), 1 billion relationships (400 million `USES`, 600 million `TRANSFERRED_TO`), and about one property record per node and per relationship.
steps.code:
nodes          120,000,000    15 bytes each   546 per 8 KB page
relationships 1,000,000,000   34 bytes each   240 per page
property recs 1,120,000,000   41 bytes each   199 per page

steps.say: Turn counts into whole pages with the lab's `alignedStoreBytes`: records divided by records per page, rounded up, times 8,192. Strings longer than a property block can hold go to a separate store; leave room for them in the estimate.
steps.code:
// subgoal: store bytes per file
val gib = 1L shl 30
val nodes = alignedStoreBytes(120_000_000, NODE_RECORD_SIZE)      // 1.7 GiB
val rels = alignedStoreBytes(1_000_000_000, REL_RECORD_SIZE)     // 31.8 GiB
val props = alignedStoreBytes(1_120_000_000, 41)                 // 42.9 GiB
println((nodes + rels + props).toDouble() / gib)                 // 76.4

steps.say: Add the indexes and growth. Two range indexes on 120 million ids add a few GiB; call it 80 GiB. The page cache should hold all of it plus 20%: 96 GiB. Relationships and properties, not nodes, are most of the store.
steps.code:
store + indexes   about 80 GiB
page cache        80 x 1.2 = 96 GiB
heap              31 GiB (the most that keeps compressed oops)
operating system  about 10 GiB
total             about 137 GiB

steps.say: Check the machine size with `neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation --memory=...`. For 128 GiB it gives a 31 GiB heap and an 81 GiB page cache: short of 96. For 192 GiB it gives 31 and 143, which leaves room to grow.
steps.code:
--memory=128g  ->  heap 31g, page cache 81g    (too small for 96 GiB)
--memory=192g  ->  heap 31g, page cache 143g   (fits, with growth)

steps.say: Write it down as settings, with the page cache set from the store rather than the heuristic, and the log on its own disk. With three primaries, every server gets the same memory, because any of them can become the writer.

lab.title: Build Neo4j's record store: fixed-size records, relationship chains and a walk
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. One test passes, because it tests the given `locate`; seven fail.
Write `alignedStoreBytes`: whole pages, at least one. The test checks it against the file sizes Neo4j wrote in the Try-its, 8,192 bytes for 28 nodes and 73,728 for 2,037 relationships.

Write `createRelationship`, following the KDoc: link the new record in at the head of both chains, store the degree in the head's prev field, and fix up the old head. Then a test rebuilds the fraud graph in Neo4j's creation order and compares your records with the bytes `od` showed in the first Try-it.

Write `relationshipsOf` (walk one chain), `degree` (two reads) and `expand` (a breadth-first walk). The last test adds 100,000 unrelated transfers and checks that your walk reads exactly as many records as before, while the link-table model's index lookups get three times as deep. All eight pass.
hints: `alignedStoreBytes`: `val perPage = PAGE_SIZE / recordSize`, then `max(1L, (records + perPage - 1) / perPage) * PAGE_SIZE`.

In `createRelationship`, write a local `fun linkIn(node: Long): Pair<Long, Long>` that returns (degree, next) for the new record, and call it for `from`, then `to`. Use `old.copy(firstPrev = id, firstInFirstChain = false)` (or the second pair) to rewrite the old head.

Read the old head inside `linkIn`, after the call for `from` has finished. If the last relationship you created joined the same two nodes, both calls touch the same record, and the second must see the first one's write.
In a chain, the node is either `rel.firstNode` or `rel.secondNode`: pick `firstNext` or `secondNext` (and `firstPrev` or `secondPrev`) to match.
`expand`: keep a `seen` set with the start in it, a frontier list per hop, and add a node to the result only the first time `seen.add(other)` returns true.

drill.title: A relationship record from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) list the fields of a 34-byte relationship record in Neo4j's record format; (b) A-3101 (node 2) has relationships 28, 26, 5 and 4, newest first. Write the pointers relationship 26 holds for A-3101, and say what relationship 28's prev field for A-3101 contains and why; (c) say where a commit goes first, and what happens to the store files at a checkpoint and after a crash.

answer.src:
(a) in-use byte | first node | second node | type |
    first node's prev | first node's next | second node's prev | second node's next |
    first property | flags: head of the first chain, head of the second chain
    (1 + 8 x 4 + 1 = 34 bytes)
(b) relationship 26 is A-3101 -> A-3103, so A-3101 uses the FIRST pair:
    firstPrev = 28, firstNext = 5
    relationship 28 heads A-3101's chain, so it has no prev: that field holds
    the chain's length, A-3101's degree, 4
(c) the transaction log first (appended, fsync'ed at commit), then the pages in
    the page cache. A checkpoint writes the dirty pages to the store files; after
    a crash, recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint.

recap: Neo4j's record format stores fixed-size records (nodes 15 bytes, relationships 34, properties 41) in files of 8 KB pages, so record N is at byte N x size: a hop is a multiplication and a read, whatever the size of the graph.

Each node's relationships are a doubly linked list threaded through the relationship records; each relationship sits in two chains, the newest is at the head, and the head stores the degree. Dense nodes (over 50 relationships) get one chain per type and direction. Enterprise's `block` format (default since 5.22) packs a node's data into one block; Community stays on `aligned`.

The page cache, off-heap and sized by `server.memory.pagecache.size`, should hold the store plus indexes plus 20%; the heap (initial = max, at most 31 GB) holds queries, plans and transaction state. `neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation` gives a starting split.

A commit is appended and fsync'ed to the transaction log, then applied in the page cache; checkpoints (15 minutes or 100,000 transactions, and on shutdown) write the store files, and recovery replays the log after a crash. Indexes only find the starting nodes.

Community is one server with one user database; back it up offline with `neo4j-admin database dump`. Enterprise adds online backups and clusters: primaries agree with Raft (2F + 1 to survive F failures), secondaries pull the log to scale reads, and `neo4j://` drivers route by a routing table.

quiz.q: The fraud graph grows from 1 million to 1 billion relationships. A query walks A-3101's four relationships from its node record. How many record reads does that part of the walk take now?
options: About 3 times as many, like a B+tree that gained levels
The same five: one for the node, one per relationship
Twice as many, because each relationship is in two chains
It depends on whether the relationship type has an index
quiz.why: Record N is at byte N x 34, so reading the next relationship in a chain is arithmetic on its id, and the chain has as many records as the node has relationships. The size of the rest of the graph never enters. A B+tree lookup does get deeper as the table grows, which is the tempting answer. Being in two chains doesn't double anything: the walk follows one of the two pointer pairs. Relationships are never found through an index.

quiz.q: Neo4j is killed by the OOM killer 10 minutes after its last checkpoint. Thousands of transactions committed in those 10 minutes. What happens when it starts again?
options: Those transactions are lost: the store files only have the last checkpoint
Neo4j replays the transaction log from the last checkpoint, and every committed transaction is back
Neo4j refuses to start until you run `neo4j-admin database check`
Only the transactions that were still in the page cache are lost
quiz.why: A commit returns only after its changes are appended to the transaction log and forced to disk. The store files are behind, by up to one checkpoint interval, and recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint to close the gap, as the Try-it showed with "1 transactions applied". The page cache is lost in a crash, but nothing committed lived only there. `check` verifies consistency; recovery doesn't need it.

quiz.q: A server has 64 GB of RAM. The store and indexes take 40 GB and grow about 10% a year. Which setting is the sound start?
options: heap 48 GB, page cache 8 GB: queries need memory
heap 31 GB, page cache 31 GB
heap 12 GB, page cache 48 GB, the rest for the OS
no settings: the OS page cache will hold the store
quiz.why: The page cache should hold the whole store plus room to grow, 40 x 1.2 = 48 GB, or walks start reading from disk. The heap needs to fit the concurrent queries and transactions, and 12 GB is plenty for most; a 48 GB heap also loses compressed oops. Neo4j caches the store in its own page cache, so leaving it unset just gets a heuristic that knows nothing about your store.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: PostgreSQL finds a row by (page, slot) through the line pointer array at the top of the page; Neo4j finds relationship 28 at byte 28 x 34. What does the slotted page give PostgreSQL that Neo4j's fixed-size records don't?
options: Rows of any length: a line pointer lets a row of any size sit anywhere in the page, and move when the page is compacted, while its (page, slot) address stays the same
Faster lookups, because reading a line pointer is quicker than multiplying
Crash safety, because line pointers make the write-ahead log unnecessary
Nothing, because both layouts can only store rows of one size
quiz.why: Fixed-size records make the address arithmetic, which is why a Neo4j hop costs a multiplication; the price is that anything longer than a record, such as a long string, must spill into other records and cost extra reads. A slotted page adds one level of indirection so rows can vary in size and move inside the page without changing their address. Both layouts still need a log for crash safety, and neither lookup is slow.

quiz.q: A Quarkus service connects to a three-primary cluster with `bolt://graph-2:7687`. graph-2 is a follower. What happens to its write transactions, and what's the fix?
options: graph-2 forwards them to the writer, so nothing
They fail, because a direct bolt connection doesn't route; use a neo4j:// address so the driver fetches a routing table
They are written to graph-2 and replicated later
They block until graph-2 becomes the writer
quiz.why: `bolt://` means one specific server, and a follower doesn't accept writes. With `neo4j://` the driver fetches a routing table (writers, readers, routers, with a TTL) and sends each write transaction to the current writer, even after a new election. Writing to a follower and replicating later would break Raft's guarantee that every commit is on a majority.

flashcards.front: How big are Neo4j's node, relationship and property records in the record format?
flashcards.back: 15, 34 and 41 bytes. Record N starts at byte N x size, so no index is needed to find it.

flashcards.front: What does a relationship record point to?
flashcards.back: Its two nodes, its type, the previous and next relationship in the first node's chain, the same for the second node's chain, and its first property record.

flashcards.front: Why can Neo4j count a node's relationships in two reads?
flashcards.back: The head of a chain has no previous record, so that field stores the chain's length, the node's degree.

flashcards.front: Page cache vs heap in Neo4j?
flashcards.back: Page cache: off-heap, holds the store and index pages, size it to store + indexes + 20%. Heap: queries, plans, transaction state; initial = max, at most 31 GB.

flashcards.front: Where does a commit go first, and what does a checkpoint do?
flashcards.back: Appended and fsync'ed to the transaction log, then applied in the page cache. A checkpoint writes dirty pages to the store files, so recovery replays the log from there.

flashcards.front: How do you back up Neo4j Community?
flashcards.back: Stop the server and run `neo4j-admin database dump`; restore with `load`. Online backup is Enterprise only.
neo4j:// fetches a routing table and sends writes to the cluster's writer and reads to readers. bolt:// talks to one server only.

explain_back.prompt: An SRE who runs your Oracle databases is about to run Neo4j for the fraud team. Explain how Neo4j stores the graph, what the page cache and heap are for and how to size them, what happens on a crash, and what Community gives you compared with a cluster.
explain_back.answer: Neo4j's Community store keeps fixed-size records in files: nodes are 15 bytes, relationships 34, properties 41. Record N is at byte N times the record size, so following a relationship is arithmetic on an id, not an index lookup, and it costs the same however big the graph gets. Each node's relationships are a doubly linked list threaded through the relationship records, newest first, and each relationship sits in two of those lists. Indexes are only used to find where a walk starts. Neo4j reads the files through its own page cache, an off-heap buffer pool of 8 KB pages; I'd size it to the store plus indexes plus 20%, because a walk that misses goes to disk a thousand times slower. The heap holds queries and uncommitted transactions; set initial equal to max and stay at or under 31 GB. Commits work like Oracle's redo: they're appended and fsync'ed to the transaction log, the store files catch up at checkpoints every 15 minutes or 100,000 transactions, and after a crash Neo4j replays the log from the last checkpoint. Community is one server with one user database, and backups mean stopping it and running neo4j-admin database dump. Enterprise adds online backups and clusters: three primaries agree with Raft and survive one failure, secondaries pull the log to scale reads, and drivers with neo4j:// URLs route writes to the current writer.

deeper.body:
Property records are where most of the store goes, and they hide a second level. Each 41-byte record has four 8-byte blocks. A small integer or a short string fits in one or two blocks inline. A longer string or an array spills into `neostore.propertystore.db.strings` or `.arrays`, as a chain of dynamic records, so a long merchant name costs extra record reads. Property keys aren't stored as text either: `amountMinor` is a token id, and the names live in `neostore.propertystore.db.index.keys`.
Ids are reused. When you delete a node, its id goes on a free list (the `.id` files next to each store), and a later `CREATE` can get the same id. Any code that stored `id(n)` outside the database can then point at a different node. That's why the Try-it used `id()` only to find the bytes, and why Cypher 5 and 25 prefer `elementId()`, which is only guaranteed within one transaction anyway. Use your own key, such as `Account.id`, with a uniqueness constraint.

The `block` format was built to cut the pointer chasing this lesson walked through. In the record format, reading one node with its labels, properties and relationships can touch three or four files. In `block`, a node's small block (128 bytes, split into two 64-byte records) holds labels, inlined properties under about 31 bytes, and relationships, so one page read usually gets all of it. Bigger nodes spill into dynamic blocks of up to 8 KB, and dense nodes keep their relationships in a B+tree sorted by type and direction. Moving an Enterprise database is `neo4j-admin database migrate --to-format=block`, offline, and it changes internal ids. The `standard` and `high_limit` formats are deprecated, and the manual plans to end their support in November 2029.

Watching the page cache is an Enterprise feature in practice. Enterprise's metrics include `page_cache.hits`, `page_cache.page_faults` and `page_cache.hit_ratio`. On Community 2026.10, `PROFILE` prints a "Page Cache Hits/Misses" column that the default slotted runtime leaves at 0/0, and `dbms.queryJmx` returns only the JVM's own beans, so the signs of a page cache that's too small are indirect: walks that slow down as the store grows, and disk reads on the store files while queries run.

Clusters also decide where each database lives. A server can host some databases as a primary and others as a secondary, and `CREATE DATABASE ... TOPOLOGY 3 PRIMARIES 2 SECONDARIES` sets the copies per database. The `system` database, which holds users and the list of databases, has its own Raft group across the servers set with `server.cluster.system_database_mode`. One elected writer per database means writes to different databases can go to different servers.
